name: Wren Ashdown
epithet: Runner and ledger-keeper of Saint Ysolde's
appearance: Twenty-one, wiry and sharp-faced, with ink on her hands and a pencil behind her ear. She walked beside Darrow's litter up the Thousand Steps in the cliff wind without once losing the count, and on the first snow of the year she stood in the infirmary doorway out of breath, snow on the shoulders of her cloak, her cheeks red from the wind and the rest of her face white, her ledger clutched to her chest like a shield. She talks fast and irreverently, with a number in every third sentence and a 'technically' ready whenever she is about to disagree with you.
last_seen_doing: Standing in the infirmary doorway with the news of the riders, answering Hollis's question of who was first on the list by looking at Darrow instead of speaking, before she went back to the bell tower.
now: She has gone back up to the bell tower, where Sister Pell's glass looks down on the Holloway and the six grey-cloaked riders with their cart and smoking censer, who will be at the foot of the Steps by tomorrow night if the snow holds off. Mother Ione has been told. The whole House knows there is a list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's; Wren knows its order.
story_so_far: She counted every one of the Thousand Steps aloud beside Darrow's litter on the day the lay brothers carried him up to Saint Ysolde's, insisting there are eleven hundred and seventeen and that everyone who says a thousand is wrong. Her ledgers keep the House's tallies: the Steps, the cots, the bells, and how many times the captain of the Ninth has asked to go down the mountain and how many times Mender Vorne has said no. Seven weeks after the Binding, on the first snow of the year, she ran down from the bell tower to the infirmary hall with word of six grey cloaks and a censer on the Holloway road, and of a list read out at the inn in Coldmere naming the Faithless they had come to bring down to kneel. Hollis is second on it. When he asked who was first, she looked at Darrow.

quote.text: There's eleven hundred and seventeen. Everyone says a thousand. Everyone's wrong.

known_facts.fact: She walked beside Darrow's litter up the Thousand Steps counting every step aloud, and did not stop until the top.
By her count there are eleven hundred and seventeen Steps, not a thousand, and she holds that everyone who says a thousand is wrong.
When Darrow, feverish on the litter, told her she had missed a step, she denied it and went on counting.
When the bells of the House ring the hour, she is somewhere inside counting them.

Her ledgers record the Steps, the cots and how many are full, the day's bells, and the number of times the captain of the Ninth has asked to go down the Steps against the number of times Mender Vorne has refused him.
She told Darrow that Maelis says 'Time makes it possible, proof makes it permitted' in her sleep; Maelis says she does not sleep and that Wren lies, which Wren calls embellishing.
From the bell tower, through Sister Pell's glass, she watches the Holloway road.

She brought the infirmary hall the news of six grey-cloaked riders and a cart on the Holloway, with a censer smoking in the snow, expected at the foot of the Steps by tomorrow night if the snow holds off.
She knows the order of the list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's that was read out at the inn in Coldmere: Hollis is second, and when he asked who was first she answered only by looking at Darrow.

relationships.label: the captain she counted up the Steps
relationships.note: She counted the Steps aloud beside his litter the day he was carried up, keeps a tally of every time he has asked to go down them, and when Hollis asked who was first on the Confessors' list, she looked at Darrow instead of answering.

relationships.label: Mender Vorne
relationships.note: Wren claims Maelis says her saying in her sleep; Maelis says she does not sleep and that Wren lies, and Wren calls it embellishing.

relationships.label: the second name on the list
relationships.note: She was the one who told him he was second on the list the Confessors read out in Coldmere.

deeper: The count never stops, even when she sleeps.
